title: Worker barred from using AI in complaint against boss
full_text:
Australia’s workplace umpire has taken the unprecedented step of banning a worker from using artificial intelligence to draft complaints against her employer, in a sign courts and tribunals are moving to stem a wave of AI-generated legal disputes swamping businesses.
The Fair Work Commission handed down the orders last week preventing a caretaker working for a body corporate on Queensland’s Sunshine Coast from using AI technology because it resulted in lengthy, repetitive and accusatory emails that worsened her otherwise justified bullying complaint.
The order is the first to address AI in the Fair Work Act’s broad anti-bullying jurisdiction and suggests similar cases could be coming as bosses complain about having to respond to countless pages of AI-generated slop.
Commissioner Sarah McKinnon found the caretaker was subject to bullying that led to a stressful workplace, including defamatory emails about her which were sent to owners, and the chair of the body corporate keeping a diary about her appearance.
However, the commissioner said the caretaker’s correspondence with the body corporate appeared to be prepared by AI and was “lengthy, wide-ranging, replete with generalisations, repetitive, and often couched in accusatory language”.
“It is unsurprising that the committee eventually chose not to engage with [the caretaker] in response,” she said.
“Unfortunately, its choice to ‘disengage and dig in’ … had the result that it did not engage in any meaningful way with many of the concerns [the caretaker] was raising.”
McKinnon ordered that all future communications be brief, accurate and respectful and “there is to be no use of AI tools in the preparation of correspondence between the parties”.
Gadens employment partner George Haros said such directives may become more common, as “in almost any form of communication with employees there is now an element of AI”.
“We’re seeing a lot of rules and regulations and directives by courts and tribunals being upfront about the use of AI – you’d think the natural progression would be to do what the commission has done here and recommend it not be used, or at least limit its use,” he said.
Senior workplace lawyers have also called for reforms to stop AI-generated claims after the Federal Circuit Court recorded its steepest annual rise in dismissal claims last year and the Federal Court had a 125 per cent increase in self-represented litigants in its workplace jurisdiction.
Barrister Ian Latham, who has represented workers and unions, proposed bans on AI and changes to the Fair Work Act’s long-standing costs shield that means parties bear their own costs regardless of who loses.
In a speech to be delivered this weekend, Latham said he had seen dozens of AI-generated submissions that “all show the danger of a little knowledge” and were creating “significant challenges” to the legal profession.
He had even heard of a witness providing evidence by audiovisual link who had used AI to provide their answers to questions, although with a slight delay.
He suggested courts and tribunals should be given more powers – possibly interim while AI evolves – to impose costs on individuals in dismissal cases or adopt more rigorous approaches to costs for unreasonable conduct.
The Fair Work Act’s costs shield was for “purely historical” reasons, he argued, that harkened back to arbitration of industrial disputes or battles within unions, but now applied to individual employees taking direct legal action against their employers.
“That creates a clear incentive to use a robot rather than a lawyer,” he said.
He recommended “express prohibitions on the use of AI in pleadings, submissions and evidence” and expanded powers to dismiss applications without assessing every AI-generated claim.
Australian Resources and Energy Employers Association chief executive Steve Knott said, “the general protections regime has become one of the biggest engines of unmeritorious litigation in Australian legal history”.
“Plenty of these claims have less prospect of success than a screen door on a submarine,” he said.
“Employers who successfully defend a claim that a tribunal has already flagged as meritless should be able to seek their costs back. Full stop. The current shield protects the reckless and punishes the vindicated.”
Australian Industry Group chief executive Innes Willox said “enhancing the ability of the courts and commission to make a costs order against a party inappropriately or dishonestly using AI should be considered as a priority to clamp down on its use”.
